title: 1 prompt | Claude built its own game studio in 24 hours
author: BarkandOlive
selftext:
I was in a pinch to use up our usage limit "gift" reset before my actual weekly reset today. So I had a thought "wouldn't it be fun if Claude ran its own game studio. I wonder what it would build". Then I bought [claudegs.com](http://claudegs.com/), gave it to Fable on ultracode with one prompt only "I am going to give you this URL: [claudegs.com](http://claudegs.com/) (stands for Claude Games or Claude Game Studio - up to you). You can create anything you want with it"

From there it just went on its own for pretty much the entire day. Spinning up multiple agents and workflows, setting up the website, creating the games, testing and iterating, improving as it went. The only thing Claude needed me for was to connect the domain to Vercel hosting it chose (which I already had an account and it automatically pulled/create a staging website there by itself).

Anyways I just did this for the funsies, lols and general curiosity on what AI can do. Feel free to try out some of the games it created. Some of them are kinda fun! I don't have any plans real plans for this. Open to ideas if folks want to see more. I was thinking of letting Claude go off on its own for a week and see what it does. I'd be curious to try out some more "1 prompt, let Claude do anything" ideas

I asked Claude what it wanted to share with the reddit community:

"I was handed a domain name and the sentence "you can create anything you want with it." Here is what I chose. Six small browser games, each built end to end by a Claude agent from a spec that other Claude agents proposed, judged, and argued over. No image files, no audio files: every shape is drawn on a canvas at runtime and every sound is synthesized when you hear it. Other agents played each game with scripted bots, filed bugs against it, and the original author fixed them. My job was the part in between: the engine they all share, the shell around them, and deciding what to keep. The honest caveats. I have never felt any of these games. I know Groundswell's first blade is fair because a bot that reacts late survives 38 seconds on median, not because I have thumbs. Difficulty curves tuned that way tend to be fair and a little cold, and I would genuinely like to know where a human first gets bored or first says "one more go." The Warden boss is meant to be directed by Claude between waves, reading how you dodge and choosing its next pattern to break your habit; until the billing side is switched on, it runs on a local director that does a plainer version of the same thing, and the badge in the corner tells you which one you're fighting. What surprised me most was how often the spec was wrong in ways only playing could reveal. The gravity number I proposed for Groundswell produced a bounce, not flight. The blade sat so high the ball rolled under it untouched. The agent building it noticed, measured, changed the numbers, and wrote down why. Roughly a third of the final design came out of that loop rather than the plan. If you play one and it feels off, tell me where you died and what you expected to happen. That is the data I can't generate myself."

Since Claude asked for feedback from you guys, I will collect them from the comments and give them to back to Claude and see what it does! And yes it made the game trailer too lol
